In Chapter 14 we introduced the general logic of ANOVA and used its independent-samples variant to analyze data from a between-participants design. But like the $t$ test, ANOVA has different varieties that can be applied in different situations. In this chapter we'll introduce the **related-samples ANOVA**. Just like the related-samples $t$ test, this is for use with within-participants or matched-subjects designs. The logic of $F$ is the same; what's new is how we account for differences between people.

## Repeated measures, repeated

We spent Chapter 13 looking at data from a handful of kids who had completed a racing game twice, first alone and then against another kid. We used a related-samples $t$ test to compare the two times via difference scores, subtracting each kid's alone-race time from their competition time. The kids were generally a little faster racing against a rival. But we left a loose end. Was it the *competition* that spurred them to race quicker, or was it perhaps just practice at turning the reel? With just the two races from each kid to compare, and the competition race always coming after the solo race, we couldn't tell.

What might we do to tease apart the possible effects of practice and competition? One idea is to add another race. If the kids raced alone *twice* before competing, we could see how much they improved from one solo race to the next, before a competitor entered the picture. Then we'd see if the kid improved even more for their third race against the rival. In other words, the difference from the first solo race to the second should show any improvement due to practice alone, while any improvement in the third race should show the additional effect of competition.

In fact, Norman Triplett gave each child six timed trials, with different sequences of solo and competition trials [@triplett1898dynamogenic]. Here we'll use the first three trials from five children who all followed the same order: alone, alone, then competition. @tbl-related-anova-data shows three race times for each of five children from Triplett's reported data. (As before, I cherry-picked them from the group Triplett classified as "positively stimulated" by competition and who completed their first races in this order to make a useful teaching example, and rounded their times to whole seconds. This isn't a full reanalysis of Triplett's data.)

| Child | First alone | Second alone | Competition |
|:------|--:|--:|--:|
| Stephen M. | 51 | 50 | 43 |
| Mary W. | 56 | 53 | 46 |
| Bertha A. | 56 | 49 | 48 |
| Clyde G. | 36 | 35 | 32 |
| Lucile W. | 52 | 50 | 43 |
| $M$ | 50.20 | 47.40 | 42.40 |
| $SS$ | 272.80 | 201.20 | 153.20 |

: Times (in seconds) for five children from Triplett's study. The columns follow the order of their first three trials. {#tbl-related-anova-data}

How do we analyze all three conditions? With two scores, we simply subtracted each child's pair of times to get a single difference score. Here there are three scores per kid, making for multiple potential pairwise comparisons. We'll get to those with post-hoc tests, as we did in Chapter 14, but simple pairwise subtraction can't handle the whole set of scores in a single test. But you know what can: ANOVA. The only difference between this and what we did in Chapter 14 is the relatedness of the samples. The related-samples ANOVA allows us to quantify and set aside the differences due to that relatedness.

{{< include quizzes/15-related-anova-third-condition.qmd >}}

## Partitioning variance in related samples

Again, the idea is that some kids are just faster overall, some are slower overall. Like, check out Clyde G.'s times in @tbl-related-anova-data. Clyde was not messing around---he totally demolished the other kids' times in every one of his races. How can we extend the ANOVA logic to capture that source of variability in the data, separate from the differences between conditions and any other sources of variability?

Let's think in terms of partitioning. In Chapter 14 we split the total sum of squared deviations into between-groups and within-groups components. I said that any treatment effect contributes to differences between groups, while chance contributes both between and within groups. But I was glossing over "chance" there. I said it is made up of sampling error and any of the other reasons people's scores differ. Well, one of those other reasons is what we're talking about here: consistent individual differences between kids. @fig-partitioning-independent labels that separately.

::: {#fig-partitioning-independent}
{{< interactive-figure relatedRecapPartitionDiagram makeVariancePartitionDiagram options='{"preset":"independent-detailed","formula":false,"ariaLabel":"Diagram partitioning total variability into variance between groups, which contains any treatment effect, sampling error, and individual differences, and variance within groups, which contains sampling error and individual differences."}' fallback="Diagram partitioning total variability into variance between groups, which contains any treatment effect, sampling error, and individual differences, and variance within groups, which contains sampling error and individual differences." >}}
::::

We still just have the split of total into between groups and within groups variability. With a between-participants design and independent-samples ANOVA, that's the only split we can make. Individual differences will contribute to within groups variability, because each group is made up of a bunch of different people. And individual differences are also present in the between groups variability, because each group is a different set of unrelated participants. 

Using a within-participants design changes this, however. We will still have a bunch of different people within each condition, so individual differences contribute to within-groups variability. Clyde G.'s super-speed makes each group substantially more variable. But now the same people appear in every condition. Whatever it is about Clyde that makes him so much faster than the other kids, he brings it with him in all three races; it is consistent across groups. So the design itself eliminates individual differences as a source of variability between groups. The only things that can make the condition means differ are the treatment effect and sampling error.

As a result, we have a slight problem. Our eventual numerator and denominator for the $F$ ratio are no longer conceptually balanced. The numerator contains treatment plus sampling error, while the denominator contains sampling error plus individual differences. But the good news is that we can *mathematically* extract those individual differences from the denominator as well, separating the sampling error and the individual differences and leaving a balanced ratio with individual differences absent from both the numerator and denominator.

To do this, we partition that within-group variance into two components: error variance, labeled $MS_{\text{error}}$, and between-people variance, $MS_{\text{people}}$. As the name suggests, the error variance consists only of unpredictable error and the between-people variance consists only of the individual differences.^[I'm oversimplifying slightly. What's left in $MS_{\text{error}}$ isn't necessarily just sampling error, strictly defined. Children might respond differently to practice or competition, or have a particularly good or bad trial. Those departures from the average pattern remain in the error component.]

::: {#fig-partitioning-related}
{{< interactive-figure relatedPartitionDiagram makeVariancePartitionDiagram options='{"preset":"related","formula":false,"ariaLabel":"Diagram partitioning total variability into variance between groups, which contains any treatment effect plus remaining chance, and variance within groups, which contains remaining chance and individual differences and is further partitioned into variance between people, which contains individual differences, and error variance, which contains the remaining chance."}' fallback="Diagram partitioning total variability into variance between groups, which contains any treatment effect plus remaining chance, and variance within groups, which contains remaining chance and individual differences and is further partitioned into variance between people, which contains individual differences, and error variance, which contains the remaining chance." >}}
:::

We will still use the same numerator, $MS_{\text{between}}$, but $MS_{\text{error}}$ becomes the new denominator of the related-samples $F$ ratio. Under the null hypothesis, both estimate the same remaining variance. A difference between the population means can make the numerator larger, just as before.

## Calculating related-samples ANOVA

Happily, the math is relatively straightforward. But before we get to the new equations, let's see how we separate out the people component using the data from the five kids in @tbl-related-anova-data. As you'll see, the key is that we group the data in a new way. So far we've grouped scores by condition; when we get to the between-people component in @act-related-partition we'll group them instead by the child they belong to. 

::::: {#act-related-partition .callout-tip .interactive}
## Where the individual differences go

{{< interactive-figure relatedAnovaExplorer makeAnovaVariabilityExplorer options='{"stage":"populations","calculations":false,"controlsOpen":false,"people":["Stephen","Mary W.","Bertha","Clyde","Lucile"],"groups":[{"name":"First alone","values":[51,56,56,36,52]},{"name":"Second alone","values":[50,53,49,35,50]},{"name":"Competition","values":[43,46,48,32,43]}],"axisLabel":"Time (seconds)","personColors":[0,3,7,1,5],"xMin":30,"xMax":60,"populationSd":7.23}' fallback="Interactive diagram of five children timed in three conditions. The scores regroup into one row per child, each child's scores slide to that child's mean, and the squared deviations fill a people layer at the bottom of the within-groups sum of squares. What remains above it is error, and only the between-groups and error layers are divided by their degrees of freedom." >}}

:::: {.callout-footer}
::: {.tutorial-step data-major="scores" data-major-title="Scores" data-title="Scores" data-action='{"stage":"populations","phase":"observe","animate":false}'}
Here are the five children's times, grouped by condition. Each child contributes one score to each row, but the first step of the related-samples ANOVA treats them as independent, so at the moment the dots are colored by race type rather than by child.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="total" data-major-title="Total" data-title="Total" data-action='{"stage":"total","phase":"sum","animate":true}'}
As in Chapter 14, we start with each score's deviation from the grand mean. Squaring and adding them gives $SS_{\text{total}}$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="within" data-major-title="Within" data-title="Within" data-action='{"stage":"within","phase":"sum","animate":true}'}
Measuring deviations from each condition's own mean gives $SS_{\text{within}}$. This is still identical to what we did with the independent-samples ANOVA last chapter. The spread within each row includes individual differences---the fact that some children are generally faster than others. We'll separate that out in a moment.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="between" data-major-title="Between" data-title="Between" data-action='{"stage":"between","phase":"sum","animate":true}'}
The differences between condition means account for $SS_{\text{between}}$. We're still applying exactly the same math as in Chapter 14, but in this case, because of the within-participants design, the between groups variability does not include individual differences. That's a product of the design, not any new math.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="people" data-major-title="People" data-title="Recolour" data-action='{"stage":"people","phase":"recolour","animate":true}'}
Now for the new part. We will use the relatedness of the scores from each kid to separate the individual-differences part of the within-groups variability. First, we'll just color the dots by child. See Clyde's orange dots, all way to the left of the others?
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="people" data-major-title="People" data-title="Rows" data-action='{"stage":"people","phase":"rows","animate":true}'}
We'll regroup the scores into one row per child, to make the relatedness more visually obvious. What we'll do next is basically the same as we did to get the between groups variability, but instead of comparing condition means, we're going to compare the *children's* means.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="people" data-major-title="People" data-title="Averages" data-action='{"stage":"people","phase":"observe","animate":true}'}
Having grouped the scores by child, we find each kid's average across their three scores. If individual differences were the only source of variability---no other chance error at all---then each kid's time would be the same in every race. So we imagine that all three of their scores are equal to their own average time.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="people" data-major-title="People" data-title="Deviations" data-action='{"stage":"people","phase":"deviations","animate":true}'}
Now we find the deviation of each child's mean from the grand mean. Is this looking familiar?
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="people" data-major-title="People" data-title="Squares" data-action='{"stage":"people","phase":"squares","animate":true}'}
Next we square each deviation. Larger squares represent children whose overall times were farther from the grand mean, whether faster or slower.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="people" data-major-title="People" data-title="Sum" data-action='{"stage":"people","phase":"sum","animate":true}'}
And finally we add those squares, counting each one three times to represent the child's three scores. They add up to $SS_{\text{people}}, part of the within-groups variability we already counted.

Now we're basically done. There's a little sliver of unaccounted variability left over. That's the error component. We can find it by simply subtracting the people component from the within-groups component: $SS_{\text{error}} = SS_{\text{within}} - SS_{\text{people}}$. But let's also see how we can get it directly from the scores, to better understand what it represents.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="centre" data-major-title="Error" data-title="Centre" data-action='{"stage":"centre","phase":"shift","animate":true}'}
To quantify the left over variability, we shift each kid's cluster of scores so that each child's mean aligns with the grand mean. That's how we remove the already-accoounted-for people varaibility from the data; each child becomes exactly average, all comparable to one another without those pesky individual differences pushing them apart. Notice that Clyde doesn't look exceptional any more. But each kid's three scores still vary a bit from one another. That's the left over error.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="centre" data-major-title="Centred" data-title="Lanes" data-action='{"stage":"centre","phase":"lanes","animate":true}'}
To qantify that left over error, we put the adjusted scores back into their condition rows. The condition means are unchanged, but the spread around them is much smaller because the children no longer differ in overall speed.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="centre" data-major-title="Centred" data-title="What's left" data-action='{"stage":"centre","phase":"squares","animate":true}'}
Now we find each adjusted score's deviation from its condition mean and square it. This is the variability that remains after accounting for both the conditions and the children's overall levels.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="centre" data-major-title="Centred" data-title="Error" data-action='{"stage":"centre","phase":"sum","animate":true}'}
The squares fill the remaining part of $SS_{\text{within}}$, showing $SS_{\text{error}}$ itself. Again, we could have obtained the same answer by just subtracting $SS_{\text{people}}$ from $SS_{\text{within}}$. Or, put another way, $SS_{\text{people}} + SS_{\text{error}} = SS_{\text{within}}$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="compare" data-major-title="Compare" data-title="Partition" data-action='{"stage":"compare","phase":"partition","animate":true}'}
Now for the mean squares. $SS_{\text{total}}$ now has three parts: between groups, between people, and error.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="compare" data-major-title="Compare" data-title="Split" data-action='{"stage":"compare","phase":"split","animate":true}'}
For the $F$ ratio, we take the between-groups and error components. This whole mathematical procedure was necessary to get a denomminator that doesn't include individual differences, so we leave those behind and just use the error compoent we extracted out of the within-groups variability.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="compare" data-major-title="Compare" data-title="F" data-action='{"stage":"compare","phase":"f","animate":true}'}
As usual, we divide each sum by its degrees of freedom to get the mean squares. The numerator is the same as in an independent-samples ANOVA, but the denominator now uses only error. In this case $df_{\text{error}} = 8$. Our numerator mean square is much bigger than the new denominator mean square, so our $F$ ratio will be large.
:::
::::

:::::

### Sums of squares and degrees of freedom

So here's how we calculate this modified $F$ ratio for related-samples data.

<!-- NOTE: move this to parenthetical or footnote. These formulas assume a complete set of scores: each person contributes one score in every condition. If someone misses a condition, we can't simply leave that cell blank and carry on with the same calculation. -->

As @act-related-partition showed, the first stage of the analysis is identical to the independent-samples ANOVA we conducted in Chapter 14. The equations for $SS_{\text{total}}$, $SS_{\text{between}}$, and $SS_{\text{within}}$ are the same, and the degrees of freedom for each component are the same as well.

The only difference is that we will now split the within-groups variability into two components: between-people and error. The equation[^related-computational] for between people has the same form as $SS_{\text{between}}$, with person means in place of group means:

$$ SS_{\text{people}} = \Sigma k(M_{\text{person}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2 $$

$M_{\text{person}}$ is the mean of one person's scores across the conditions. We square each person's deviation from the grand mean and multiply by $k$, the number of conditions, since each person's mean represents $k$ scores. Then we add them up. Same idea as between groups, just regrouping the scores by person.

The final component, and the one that will become our denominator, is what's left. Anything left over after taking the individual-difference variability out of within-groups variability is the error variability, so it's easiest to find it by subtraction:

$$ SS_{\text{error}} = SS_{\text{within}} - SS_{\text{people}} $$

Or, as @act-related-partition showed, we can get the same answer directly, from each score's deviation from its group mean once that person's overall deviation from the grand mean has been taken out:

$$ SS_{\text{error}} = \Sigma (X - M_{\text{person}} - M_{\text{group}} + M_{\text{grand}})^2 $$

For each score, subtract that child's mean and add the grand mean: $X - M_{\text{person}} + M_{\text{grand}}$. Stephen's mean is 1.33 seconds above the grand mean, so we subtract 1.33 from each of his times. His first time, 51 seconds, becomes 49.67. All three of Stephen's scores move by the same amount; their differences stay the same. Then we find the deviation from the group mean, by subtracting it from the adjusted score. We've taken out overall speed without taking out the differences we're interested in, the varaibility of scores around the group mean. Squaring and adding those deviations gives the error sum of squares.

The two new components have degrees of freedom of their own. For $SS_{\text{people}}$, we computed the deviation of each person's mean from the grand mean. So that's $n$ means, deviating from a single grand mean: $df_{\text{people}} = n - 1$.[^related-matched]

Remeber that degrees of freedom are partitioned just like the sums of squares, so we can find $df_{\text{error}}$ by subtracting the degrees of freedom for the between-people component from the degrees of freedom for the within-groups component.

$$ df_{\text{error}} = df_{\text{within}} - df_{\text{people}} $$

If you wanted to figure out the error degrees of freedom directly, you could do it the same way we did for $SS_{\text{error}}$: each person's mean is a constraint on their scores, so we lose one degree of freedom per person.

<!-- explain this better -->

$$ df_{\text{error}} = (N - k) - (n - 1) = (k - 1)(n - 1) $$

[^related-matched]: In a matched-subjects design, we do the same calculation with matched sets in place of people. Each set contributes one score per condition, and $n$ counts sets. Other books may call the between-people component “between subjects” or “between participants.”

[^related-computational]: As in Chapter 14, there's also a computational version of this formula. It uses $P$, a participant total (the sum of the scores for one person), and $G$, the grand total.

    $$ SS_{\text{people}} = \Sigma \frac{P^2}{k} - \frac{G^2}{N} $$

    We'll stick with the definitional formula here too.

### Mean squares and $F$

Once we calculate the required sums of squares and degrees of freedom, the rest is easy. We calculate the mean squares by dividing each relevant sum of squares by its degrees of freedom. Then we divide the numerator by the denominator to get $F$. The numerator is the same as before; we just have to remember to use $MS_{\text{error}}$ as the denominator, rather than $MS_{\text{within}}$.

$$
\begin{align}
MS_{\text{between}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{between}}}{df_{\text{between}}} \\
MS_{\text{error}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{error}}}{df_{\text{error}}}
\end{align}
$$

$$ F = \frac{MS_{\text{between}}}{MS_{\text{error}}} $$

The interpretation of the $F$ ratio is also the same as with independent samples. A large numerator relative to the denominator is evidence against the null hypothesis. Setting aside differences between people can make the denominator smaller, giving us a more powerful test. It isn't guaranteed, though. We'll come back to that tradeoff at the end.

{{< include quizzes/15-related-anova-partitioning-variance.qmd >}}

## A related-samples ANOVA, step by step

So let's run through the hypothesis test for the five children in @tbl-related-anova-data.

### Step 1: State the hypotheses

As always, we start that hypothesis test by stating our hypotheses. The null here is that the population mean time is the same in all three conditions:

$$ H_0: \mu_{\text{first alone}} = \mu_{\text{second alone}} = \mu_{\text{competition}} $$

The alternative hypothesis is that at least one condition differs from at least one other.

### Step 2: Set the decision criteria

Step two is to determine the critical value for the test, with $\alpha = .05$. We use the same $F$ table as in Chapter 14, with the degrees of freedom for our numerator and new denominator:

$$ df_{\text{between}} = k - 1 = 2 $$

$$ df_{\text{error}} = (k - 1)(n - 1) = 2(4) = 8 $$

In @tbl-related-anova-critical, the column for 2 and the row for 8 give a critical $F$ of 4.46.

::: {#tbl-related-anova-critical}
{{< interactive-figure relatedAnovaCriticalTable makeFTable options='{"title":"Critical values for the competition test","alpha":0.05,"df1":{"from":1,"to":4},"df2":{"from":6,"to":12},"tableMinWidth":"0","maxWidth":"32rem","interactive":false,"selected":{"df1":2,"df2":8,"alpha":0.05}}' fallback="F table excerpt for numerator df 1 through 4 and denominator df 6 through 10, highlighting the .05 critical value of 4.46 at F(2, 8)." >}}

An excerpt of the $F$ table, with the critical value for $df = 2$ and $8$ highlighted.
:::

Note that if these 15 scores had come from independent samples, the denominator would have had 12 degrees of freedom and the critical value would have been 3.89. Our lower degrees of freedom mean we need a more extreme $F$ to reject the null, just as we saw with the related-samples $t$ test.

{{< include quizzes/15-related-anova-degrees-of-freedom.qmd >}}

### Step 3: Collect and analyze the data

Step three is to calculate the $F$ ratio for the data. Like the calculations for the independent-samples ANOVA, this is a little labor intensive to do by hand. But it's worth practicing to make sure you understand how to use each equation and what each component represents.

It's a good idea to use a summary table as you work through this by hand, like we did in Chapter 14. This one will just have additional rows for new sources of variance: between people and error. @tbl-related-anova-summary-blank shows the equations for each element.

::: {#tbl-related-anova-summary-blank .sfs-summary-table}
| Source | $SS$ | $df$ | $MS$ | $F$ |
|:-------|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Between groups | $\Sigma n_{\text{group}}(M_{\text{group}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | $k - 1$ | $\dfrac{SS_{\text{between}}}{df_{\text{between}}}$ | $\dfrac{MS_{\text{between}}}{MS_{\text{error}}}$ |
| Within groups | $\Sigma (X - M_{\text{group}})^2$ | $N - k$ | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |
| &emsp;Between people | $\Sigma k(M_{\text{person}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | $n - 1$ | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |
| &emsp;Error | $SS_{\text{within}} - SS_{\text{people}}$ | $(k - 1)(n - 1)$ | $\dfrac{SS_{\text{error}}}{df_{\text{error}}}$ | []{.sfs-na} |
| Total | $\Sigma (X - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | $N - 1$ | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |

A related-samples ANOVA summary table, showing each equation.
:::

To save you some trouble, @tbl-related-anova-data gives each condition's mean and sum of squares. Here are $n$, $k$, $N$, and $M_{\text{grand}}$ too. Remember that we have five children but 15 scores.

$$n = 5 \qquad k = 3 \qquad N = 15 \qquad M_{\text{grand}} = 46.67$$

<!-- include SS_between groups and SS_within groups calculations -->

The only new component we need to calculate is $SS_{\text{people}}$, since we can then find error by subtraction. The People column of @tbl-related-anova-people shows each child's mean and the squared deviation of that mean from the grand mean. Each kid's three rows get the same value, which is why the mathematical arrangement of multiplying the one squared deviation by $k$ works.

<!-- show k(dev)^2 peron equation -->

Then we can find $SS_{\text{error}}$ by subtracting $SS_{\text{people}}$ from $SS_{\text{within}}$.

<!-- show equation -->

But let's also see how one of those error squares comes from an individual score. In the tutorial, Stephen's first time went from 51 to 49.67 seconds after we removed his difference in overall speed. The first-alone mean stayed at 50.20. So his adjusted score is $49.67 - 50.20 = -0.53$ seconds from that condition's mean. This remaining deviation is called a **residual**; squaring it gives about 0.28.

That's what the longer expression in @tbl-related-anova-people does: $X - M_{\text{person}} + M_{\text{grand}}$ adjusts the score, and subtracting $M_{\text{group}}$ gives the residual. The table shows both the people squares and these error squares for every score. (I've rounded the values I'm showing to two decimal places, but the calculations use the unrounded values, so you'll need to do the same if you want your answers to match mine exactly.)

| $M_{\text{person}}=51.00$ |                   |            |                                                  |                                                                    |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Clyde G.                  | First alone       | $36$       | $(-12.33)^2=152.11$                              | $(-1.87)^2=3.48$                                                   |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           | Second&nbsp;alone | $35$       | $(-12.33)^2=152.11$                              | $(-0.07)^2=0.00$                                                   |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           | Competition       | $32$       | $(-12.33)^2=152.11$                              | $1.93^2=3.74$                                                      |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $M_{\text{person}}=34.33$ |                   |            |                                                  |                                                                    |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Lucile W.                 | First alone       | $52$       | $1.67^2=2.78$                                    | $0.13^2=0.02$                                                      |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           | Second&nbsp;alone | $50$       | $1.67^2=2.78$                                    | $0.93^2=0.87$                                                      |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           | Competition       | $43$       | $1.67^2=2.78$                                    | $(-1.07)^2=1.14$                                                   |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| $M_{\text{person}}=48.33$ |                   |            |                                                  |                                                                    |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| **Sum of squares**        |                   |            | $SS_{\text{people}}=601.33$                      | $SS_{\text{error}}=25.87$                                          |
+---------------------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+

: Each child's three scores, with the two new squared deviations. Values are rounded; the sums use unrounded values. {#tbl-related-anova-people}


Here's the full working, so you can check your answers:

<!-- break this up and move the parts above -->

$$
\begin{align}
SS_{\text{total}} &= \Sigma (X - M_{\text{grand}})^2 = 783.33 \\
SS_{\text{within}} &= \Sigma (X - M_{\text{group}})^2 \\ &= 272.80 + 201.20 + 153.20 = 627.20 \\
SS_{\text{between}} &= \Sigma n_{\text{group}}(M_{\text{group}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2 \\ &= 5(3.53)^2 + 5(0.73)^2 + 5(-4.27)^2 = 156.13 \\
SS_{\text{people}} &= \Sigma k(M_{\text{person}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2 \\ &= 5.33 + 75.00 + 56.33 + 456.33 + 8.33 = 601.33 \\
SS_{\text{error}} &= SS_{\text{within}} - SS_{\text{people}} \approx 627.20 - 601.33 \approx 25.87
\end{align}
$$

$$
\begin{align}
df_{\text{total}} &= N - 1 = 15 - 1 = 14 \\
df_{\text{within}} &= N - k = 15 - 3 = 12 \\
df_{\text{between}} &= k - 1 = 3 - 1 = 2 \\
df_{\text{people}} &= n - 1 = 5 - 1 = 4 \\
df_{\text{error}} &= (k - 1)(n - 1) = (3 - 1)(5 - 1) = 8
\end{align}
$$

$$
\begin{align}
MS_{\text{between}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{between}}}{df_{\text{between}}} = \frac{156.13}{2} = 78.07 \\
MS_{\text{error}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{error}}}{df_{\text{error}}} = \frac{25.87}{8} = 3.23
\end{align}
$$

$$ F = \frac{MS_{\text{between}}}{MS_{\text{error}}} = \frac{78.07}{3.23} \approx 24.14 $$

And here's the completed summary table:

::: {#tbl-related-anova-summary .sfs-summary-table}
| Source | $SS$ | $df$ | $MS$ | $F$ |
|:-------|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Between groups | 156.13 | 2 | 78.07 | 24.14 |
| Within groups | 627.20 | 12 | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |
| &emsp;Between people | 601.33 | 4 | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |
| &emsp;Error | 25.87 | 8 | 3.23 | []{.sfs-na} |
| Total | 783.33 | 14 | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |

Completed related-samples ANOVA summary table for the competition example.
:::

### Step 4: Make a decision

So now we've calculated our $F$ ratio, we're ready to make our decision. We compare it to the critical value we found in the table, and if our $F$ ratio is bigger than the critical value, we reject the null hypothesis. Here with our $F$ of $24.14$, well beyond the critical value of $4.46$, we can reject the null. There is a significant difference among our three conditions. The corresponding $p$-value is about $.0004$, so $p$ is less than $\alpha$.

::: {#fig-related-anova-decision}
{{< interactive-figure relatedAnovaTestDecision makeDistributionGraph options='{"color":"var(--sfs-null-color, currentColor)","distribution":"f","df1":2,"df2":8,"title":"Null distribution: F(2, 8)","style":"minimal","xAxis":true,"yLabel":false,"xDomain":[0,27],"xTicks":6,"labels":{"x":"F ratio"},"shade":{"tail":"right","alpha":0.05},"markers":[{"at":4.45897,"label":"4.46","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-critical-color, #c63f3f)"},{"at":24.14433,"label":"F = 24.14","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-accent, #2c7fb8)"}],"maxWidth":"42rem"}' fallback="Null F distribution with 2 and 8 degrees of freedom. The rejection region lies above 4.46; the observed F of 24.14 is far into the rejection region." >}}

The observed $F = 24.14$ falls beyond the critical value of the null $F$ distribution with $df = 2$ and $8$.
:::

{{< include quizzes/15-related-anova-calculate-f.qmd >}}

### Step 5: Estimate the effect, compare the conditions, and consider power

#### Effect size: partial $\eta^2$

In Chapter 14 we used $\eta^2$, the between-groups sum of squares as a proportion of the total. Here we'll use **partial eta squared**, $\eta^2_p$. It asks what proportion is between groups once we've set aside the between-people component.

Think of the bucket again. Leave the people layer behind, and the remaining total is $SS_{\text{between}} + SS_{\text{error}}$. That's the same as $SS_{\text{total}} - SS_{\text{people}}$. So:

$$\eta^2_p = \frac{SS_{\text{between}}}{SS_{\text{between}} + SS_{\text{error}}} = \frac{156.13}{156.13 + 25.87} = .86$$

About 86% of that remaining variability is between conditions. Ordinary $\eta^2$ would still be possible, but would give a different answer, $.20$, because it includes the large people component in the denominator.

#### Post-hoc tests

The ANOVA tells us the population means aren't all equal, but not which ones differ. We can follow it with Tukey's HSD, as in Chapter 14, protecting our experimentwise $\alpha$ while comparing all three pairs.

The procedure is the same, but we use $MS_{\text{error}}$ and its degrees of freedom. In @tbl-related-anova-q, find the column for three conditions and the row for $df_{\text{error}} = 8$. Their intersection gives the critical studentized range value, $q = 4.04$, for $\alpha = .05$.

::: {#tbl-related-anova-q}
{{< interactive-figure relatedAnovaTukeyTable makeTukeyTable options='{"title":"Tukey critical values for the competition test","alpha":0.05,"k":{"from":2,"to":6},"df":{"from":4,"to":10},"tableMinWidth":"0","cellMinWidth":"0","maxWidth":"36rem","interactive":false,"selected":{"k":3,"df":8,"alpha":0.05}}' fallback="Studentized range critical values at alpha .05 for 2 through 6 conditions and error df 4 through 10. The highlighted cell for 3 conditions and 8 error degrees of freedom is q = 4.04." >}}

Critical values of $q$ for $\alpha = .05$. The column gives the number of conditions; the row gives the error degrees of freedom.
:::

And $n = 5$, the number of scores in each condition:

$$HSD = q \sqrt{\frac{MS_{\text{error}}}{n}} = 4.04 \sqrt{\frac{3.23}{5}} \approx 3.25$$

So a difference between means greater than 3.25 seconds is significant at the $.05$ level.

| Comparison | Absolute difference | Exceeds 3.25 seconds? |
|:--|--:|:--:|
| First alone vs. second alone | 2.80 seconds | No |
| Second alone vs. competition | 5.00 seconds | Yes |
| First alone vs. competition | 7.80 seconds | Yes |

The two gaps involving competition exceed the HSD, but the gap between the solo trials doesn't. The children improved by an average of 2.80 seconds before competing, and by another 5.00 seconds when competition began. Only the comparisons involving competition are significant.

## Reporting and interpreting results

So finally, we're ready to report the results. As usual, you need descriptives for each condition; a statement of what test was performed and whether it was significant; the test statistic itself with degrees of freedom; $p$ compared to $\alpha$; and effect size. And here we include a summary of the post-hoc tests stating which conditions differed significantly and nonsignificantly.

> In this selected five-child example, a single-factor, related-samples ANOVA revealed a significant difference among children's times on their first race alone ($M = 50.20$, $SD = 8.26$ seconds), a second race alone ($M = 47.40$, $SD = 7.09$ seconds), and a race in competition ($M = 42.40$, $SD = 6.19$ seconds); $F(2, 8) = 24.14$, $p < .001$, $\eta^2_p = .86$. Tukey HSD comparisons indicated that children were significantly faster in competition than on either solo trial. The two solo trials did not differ significantly.

What kind of graph would work best to visualize results like these? We mentioned in Chapter 14 that bar graphs with error bars are common, but they can emphasize some features of the data and can hide others. A simple bar graph showing condition means with confidence intervals wouldn't convey the relatedness of the scores. Really we're interested in how consistently each child's time changed across the conditions, rather than treating the conditions as independent.

But if you graphed the condition means in the usual way, the result might look surprising. The confidence intervals in @fig-related-results overlap, even though both comparisons involving competition were significant.

::: {#fig-related-results}
{{< interactive-figure relatedResultsGraph makeGraph options='{"type":"interval","orientation":"vertical","mark":"bar","data":[{"label":"First alone","estimate":50.2,"lower":39.9459,"upper":60.4541,"color":"var(--sfs-text, #222)"},{"label":"Second alone","estimate":47.4,"lower":38.5938,"upper":56.2062,"color":"var(--sfs-text, #222)"},{"label":"Competition","estimate":42.4,"lower":34.7157,"upper":50.0843,"color":"var(--sfs-text, #222)"}],"yDomain":[0,70],"yTickValues":[0,20,40,60],"width":640,"height":380,"margin":{"top":22,"right":16,"bottom":65,"left":65},"showValues":false,"labels":{"x":"Condition","y":"Mean time (seconds)"},"ariaLabel":"Mean times: first alone 50.20 seconds, second alone 47.40, and competition 42.40. Error bars are 95 percent confidence intervals for each condition mean, calculated from its own standard deviation. All three intervals overlap."}' fallback="Mean times: first alone 50.20 seconds, second alone 47.40, and competition 42.40. Error bars are 95 percent confidence intervals for each condition mean, calculated from its own standard deviation. All three intervals overlap." >}}

A bar graph showing average times in the three conditions. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals for each condition's mean, each calculated from that condition's own standard deviation ($df = 4$).
:::

Those intervals describe uncertainty about each condition's mean separately. They still reflect how much the children differ from one another. They don't show how consistently each child's time changed.

@fig-related-profiles makes that visible. Each line follows one child across the conditions. Every line falls at both steps, even though the children start at quite different levels. The graph follows the order in which all five children experienced the conditions.

::: {#fig-related-profiles}
{{< interactive-figure relatedProfileLines makeProfileLines options='{"categories":["First alone","Second alone","Competition"],"series":[{"name":"Stephen","color":0,"values":[51,50,43]},{"name":"Mary W.","color":3,"values":[56,53,46]},{"name":"Bertha","color":7,"values":[56,49,48]},{"name":"Clyde","color":1,"values":[36,35,32]},{"name":"Lucile","color":5,"values":[52,50,43]}],"yDomain":[30,60],"yLabel":"Time (seconds)","xLabel":"Condition","ariaLabel":"One line per child across the three conditions. Every line falls from first alone to second alone and again to competition, and the lines stay in much the same order."}' fallback="One line per child across the three conditions. Every line falls at each step." >}}

The same data, with one line for each child.
:::

To put confidence intervals around the changes themselves, we can use the difference scores for each pair of conditions, just as in Chapter 13. Now the differences in overall speed are out of the picture. The interval for the solo-to-solo change in @fig-related-differences includes zero; the two involving competition don't. These are ordinary 95% paired intervals, though, not adjusted for multiple comparisons like Tukey's test. They also use each pair's own variability rather than the pooled error term, so they needn't always agree with Tukey's decisions.

For example, subtracting each child's second-alone time from their competition time gives differences of $-7$, $-7$, $-1$, $-3$, and $-7$ seconds. Their mean is $M_D = -5.00$ and their standard deviation is $s_D = \sqrt{8} = 2.83$. With five children, the standard error is $s_{M_D} = s_D/\sqrt{n} = 1.26$ seconds. Using the two-tailed critical $t = 2.776$ for $df = 4$, the 95% interval is:

$$M_D \pm t_{\text{critical}}s_{M_D} = -5.00 \pm 2.776\sqrt{\frac{8}{5}} \approx [-8.51, -1.49]$$

The calculation uses unrounded values. Both limits are negative: the interval runs from a decrease of 8.51 seconds to a decrease of 1.49 seconds.

::: {#fig-related-differences}
{{< interactive-figure relatedDifferencesGraph makeGraph options='{"type":"interval","orientation":"horizontal","data":[{"label":"First to second alone","estimate":-2.8,"lower":-5.8917,"upper":0.2917},{"label":"Second to competition","estimate":-5,"lower":-8.512,"upper":-1.488},{"label":"First to competition","estimate":-7.8,"lower":-10.6314,"upper":-4.9686}],"xDomain":[-12,2],"xTickValues":[-12,-8,-4,0],"reference":0,"margin":{"left":164},"width":640,"height":240,"showValues":false,"labels":{"x":"Mean change in time (seconds)"},"ariaLabel":"Mean changes with 95 percent confidence intervals: first to second alone, minus 2.80 seconds, from minus 5.89 to 0.29; second alone to competition, minus 5.00, from minus 8.51 to minus 1.49; first alone to competition, minus 7.80, from minus 10.63 to minus 4.97. Only the solo-to-solo interval includes zero."}' fallback="Mean changes with 95 percent confidence intervals: first to second alone, minus 2.80 seconds, from minus 5.89 to 0.29; second alone to competition, minus 5.00, from minus 8.51 to minus 1.49; first alone to competition, minus 7.80, from minus 10.63 to minus 4.97. Only the solo-to-solo interval includes zero." >}}

95% confidence intervals for the mean change between each pair of conditions, calculated from each pair's difference scores as in @fig-related-ci. These intervals aren't adjusted for multiple comparisons.
:::

### Interpreting the results

The larger improvement when competition began fits the idea that a rival helped the children speed up. But a nonsignificant solo-to-solo comparison doesn't mean practice had no effect. And a significant change after a nonsignificant one doesn't establish that the two changes differ. The times suggest a story; the tests haven't proved that story.

There's also the order problem. Both solo trials came before any competition, so their difference can't reflect a lingering effect of racing against someone. But competition always came third. We don't know how fast these children would have gone on a third trial alone. Further practice could explain some or all of the improvement we attributed to competition.

Triplett varied the order across children, as we saw in Chapter 13. Including both orders would help keep competition from always benefiting from coming later, though competing might itself affect a subsequent solo trial [@triplett1898dynamogenic]. We've used just one order to keep the worked example easy to follow; that makes its causal interpretation more limited.

Finally, these are five deliberately selected children from the part of Triplett's table labeled “stimulated positively.” Across all 20 children who followed this same order, the first-to-second-alone improvement averages 3.36 seconds, and the next improvement, when competition begins, 2.47 seconds. Our five make a particular pattern easy to see; they don't establish its size or significance in the wider population. As usual, the design and the selection of data matter as much as the calculation.

<!-- (This isn't a perfect solution, since the third race would still be after two solo races, but it would give us more information than we had before.)
That would give us more information about practice, though it still wouldn't tell us how much further practice alone would have helped on the third trial. -->

### Assumptions

The same basic considerations apply as before, with some changes for related samples. We expect scores from the same child to be related; different children's responses should be independent of one another. And as with the related-samples $t$ test, normality concerns the within-person differences we're analyzing, rather than simply the scores in each condition.

With three or more conditions, we also need **sphericity**: the population variances of the difference scores should be the same for every pair of conditions. This is different from Chapter 14's homogeneity of variance assumption: here we're comparing the variances of the *differences*, rather than the variances of the scores in each condition. Put concretely, children's first-to-second-alone changes should be about as variable as their second-alone-to-competition changes and their first-alone-to-competition changes. We're using one pooled error term for all those comparisons, so it needs to represent them reasonably well.

Our five children's difference variances are 6.2 for first to second alone, 8.0 for second alone to competition, and 5.2 for first alone to competition. Those are fairly similar. When sphericity doesn't hold, the usual test can reject the null too often. Software can apply a correction, such as Greenhouse–Geisser, which adjusts the degrees of freedom and $p$-value without changing $F$ itself.[^related-sphericity] With only two conditions, there's just one set of difference scores, so sphericity isn't an issue.

[^related-sphericity]: Software often provides Mauchly's test of sphericity, though a nonsignificant result doesn't guarantee the assumption holds, especially with a small sample. Greenhouse–Geisser uses a value called epsilon to adjust the degrees of freedom; values near 1 indicate little adjustment. Here epsilon is $.94$ and the corrected $p$ is about $.0006$, so the decision is unchanged. Follow-up comparisons also need an appropriate method if sphericity is doubtful.

## Back to two conditions

To finish, let's return to the five children and two conditions from Chapter 13, in @tbl-triplett. We analyzed those times with a related-samples $t$ test, and then saw what would happen if we ignored the pairs and used an independent-samples test. What happens if we use ANOVA instead?

Just what you might expect after Chapter 14: $F = t^2$. Ignoring the pairs gives $F(1, 8) = 0.97$, the square of the independent-samples $t$ before rounding. Using the pairs gives $F(1, 4) = 8.47$, the square of our related-samples $t$. Each has the same $p$-value as its corresponding two-tailed $t$ test. We're expressing the same evidence in a different way, not getting a second confirmation of it.

### The advantages of treating scores as related

Compare the first two columns of @tbl-related-analyses. The condition means haven't changed, so neither has the numerator. But almost all the within-groups variability turns out to be between children. Taking it out leaves a much smaller error component. Even after allowing for the lost degrees of freedom, the denominator falls from 99 to 11.35, and $F$ grows from 0.97 to 8.47.

The two approaches remove the same differences in overall speed. The $t$ test does it by subtracting each child's two times; ANOVA identifies a separate people component. With two conditions, its error sum of squares is exactly half the sum of squares of the difference scores: $90.8/2 = 45.4$.

| | Ignoring the pairs | Using the pairs | Pairs scrambled |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| $SS_{\text{between}}$ | 96.10 | 96.10 | 96.10 |
| $SS_{\text{within}}$ | 792.00 | 792.00 | 792.00 |
| $SS_{\text{people}}$ | | 746.60 | 397.60 |
| $SS$ in the denominator | 792.00 | 45.40 | 394.40 |
| $df$ in the denominator | 8 | 4 | 4 |
| $MS$ in the denominator | 99.00 | 11.35 | 98.60 |
| Critical $F$ | 5.32 | 7.71 | 7.71 |
| $F$ | 0.97 | 8.47 | 0.97 |
| $t$ | $-0.99$ | $-2.91$ | $-0.99$ |
| $p$ | .353 | .044 | .379 |

: The same scores analyzed three ways. The independent-samples calculation ignores the known pairing; the scrambled pairs are artificial. {#tbl-related-analyses}

### What if scores aren't related?

Why does using the pairs help so much here? Because the children's scores go together: a child who was fast alone tended to be fast in competition too. If their scores didn't go together, there would be much less to gain.

Let's deliberately scramble the competition times, as in @tbl-related-scrambled. These aren't real pairings anymore. But each column still contains exactly the same scores, so its mean and spread haven't changed. Anything the independent-samples calculation can see is unchanged.

| Child | Alone | Competition |
|:------|--:|--:|
| A | 54 | 57 |
| B | 67 | 36 |
| C | 38 | 39 |
| D | 46 | 43 |
| E | 42 | 41 |
| $M$ | 49.4 | 43.2 |

: The times from Chapter 13, with the competition column scrambled so that the two columns no longer go together. {#tbl-related-scrambled}

Now look at the last column of @tbl-related-analyses. The people sum of squares is much smaller. It isn't zero: even randomly grouped scores have different averages. But once we've divided by the new degrees of freedom, $MS_{\text{error}} = 98.60$, almost the same as the original $MS_{\text{within}} = 99$. Our $F$ is back to about 0.97, while the critical value is still higher because of the lower degrees of freedom.

@fig-related-buckets shows the two partitions. With the real pairs, the people layer takes up most of the within-groups variability. With scrambled pairs, it leaves much more error behind.

::: {#fig-related-buckets}
{{< interactive-figure relatedBucketReal makeAnovaVariabilityExplorer options='{"stage":"compare","phase":"f","scores":false,"calculations":true,"controlsOpen":false,"groups":[{"name":"Alone","values":[54,67,38,46,42]},{"name":"Competition","values":[43,57,39,41,36]}],"people":["Child A","Child B","Child C","Child D","Child E"],"axisLabel":"Time (seconds)","xMin":30,"xMax":72}' fallback="The partition for Chapter 13's five children: a thick between-people layer stays in the total, leaving a thin error layer, so the between-groups mean square is far larger than the error mean square." >}}

{{< interactive-figure relatedBucketScrambled makeAnovaVariabilityExplorer options='{"stage":"compare","phase":"f","scores":false,"calculations":true,"controlsOpen":false,"groups":[{"name":"Alone","values":[54,67,38,46,42]},{"name":"Competition","values":[57,36,39,43,41]}],"people":["Child A","Child B","Child C","Child D","Child E"],"axisLabel":"Time (seconds)","xMin":30,"xMax":72}' fallback="The partition for the scrambled scores: the same total and between-groups layers, but a much thinner between-people layer, leaving a thick error layer, so the two mean squares are about the same size." >}}

The real pairs (top) and the scrambled pairs (bottom).
:::

So a related-samples design doesn't automatically make a test more powerful. It helps when the related scores tend to go together, reducing the relevant variability enough to compensate for the lost degrees of freedom. And as in Chapter 13, this isn't an invitation to try both analyses and keep the result we prefer. The design tells us which calculation is appropriate; the comparison shows why that matters.
